cardPhrasings.note: Matched in CODE and never sent to the model. Trimmed, case-folded, trailing . and ! removed, then compared for EQUALITY. Measured: the model misrouted five of the eleven suggested phrasings in every trial while filling arguments perfectly, so the shapes with no ambiguity in them do not reach it.

parsed.becauseNotThis: A comma means one PAGE was named, which has a title in it for the model to read out. Only a bare unit number is a whole unit.
As above: a comma names a page, not a unit.
No count, so there is nothing to fill `days` with and guessing one would create a number of pages nobody asked for.
parsed.example: add five more days to unit 4

fills.days: <count>, as a word up to twelve or a digit

parsed.becauseNotThis: The closing half is what makes the sentence unambiguous. Without it, 'duplicate' could mean several things and belongs with the model.
parsed.example: duplicate Unit 3, Day 2 as my next class

fills.duplicate: <page title>, with the capitals the teacher typed

parsed.shape: duplicate <page title> as my next class

cardPhrasings.parsedNote: Families the matcher PARSES rather than compares, because the number or title in them is unbounded. They are matched in code for the same reason the literals are — the whole sentence IS the request, and reading an integer or a title off a fixed shape is not a judgement anybody needs a language model for. `notThis` is the near-miss each family must REFUSE, and it is the half that stops a family swallowing requests that belong to the model.

generated.note: These top-level keys are written by `Plantoir --write-contracts` from the app's own types and will be overwritten: cardPhrasings, tools, toolSchemas. The rest — nearMisses, scenarios — is hand-written intent and is preserved.

nearMisses.note: Must NOT match — each one only looks like a card phrasing, and answering the wrong question with total confidence is worse than routing it.

note: Generated from the macOS app by `Plantoir --assist-contract`. Do not hand-edit; see contracts/README.md.

cases.name: Up walks back, Down walks forward
the half-typed line is put aside, not thrown away
cases.why: Walking back Down past the newest entry hands the teacher's own half-written sentence back exactly as it was. Losing it is the thing that makes people stop trusting the arrow keys.

cases.name: Up at the oldest entry does nothing
cases.why: Rather than wrapping round to the newest, which reads as the keyboard having misfired.

cases.name: Down with no walk under way does nothing
the same thing twice in a row is remembered once
cases.why: Testing something by running it five times should not mean five presses of Up to get past it.

cases.name: an earlier, non-adjacent repeat is left alone
cases.why: The order a teacher did things in is the thing they are scrolling through. De-duplicating across the whole list would rewrite their history rather than shorten it.

cases.name: typing ends the walk
cases.why: Once a recalled line has been edited it is a new line, and Down must not silently replace what has just been typed.

keys.note: THE SAME ON BOTH PLATFORMS — decided 2026-08-16. Not a per-platform choice: a teacher who learns Up on one machine and finds it somewhere else on the other has learned nothing. Bind the arrow keys, in the composer, exactly as the mac does.

promptHistory.note: Walking back through what the teacher has asked before, the way a Terminal does. Modelled on a Terminal deliberately, because that is what teachers compare it to, and the details a Terminal gets right are the ones people notice only when they are missing. Steps are applied in order to a fresh history; `type` means the teacher edited the box, which ends the walk.

cases.when: the box holds more than one line
cases.why: The arrows have to move the caret between those lines. History would make a multi-line prompt impossible to edit.

cases.when: there is nowhere further to walk
cases.why: Up at the oldest entry, or Down with no walk under way. Passing the key on lets the field answer it — the caret moves to the start or end of the line, which is what the key means when history has nothing to offer.

passThroughWhen.note: The two cases where the arrows must do their ORDINARY job instead — the key event is passed on to the text field rather than swallowed. A key that silently does nothing reads as a dropped keystroke.

saying: roll this section over to a new year

cases.name: a rollover asks about the website and changes none of it
cases.why: The question has to reach the line a teacher READS. It was written into the reply's detail for a while, which the mac never surfaces for a write — so the feature was invisible in the app and worked over MCP alone, behind a green suite. Asserting it in the transcript is what makes that impossible to repeat. The second line matters as much: the re-dating has already happened by the time the question appears, so a teacher who does not answer must be told plainly that the website was NOT changed, or the feature quietly recreates the defect it was built to fix.

saying: roll this section over to a new year
roll this section over onto a new website

cases.name: answering the website question on a second turn still cuts the section loose
cases.why: The answer is the SECOND turn, and by then the pages are already on their dates — so the re-date plan changes nothing, and an early return on that made the whole answer a no-op: the reply talked about dates, never mentioned the website, and left the section pinned to last year's, behind an offer that looked like it had worked. Nothing exercised two turns in a row, which is why it survived. Both turns go through the plan card here, because asking before changing is ON unless a teacher turns it off.

cases.name: deploy with a preview running
cases.why: The window's Deploy button stops any running preview first and waits for it to finish: stop mode finds a section's processes by working directory and would take the deploy's build with it.

cases.name: deploy with no preview running
cases.why: Nothing to stop. The reply says nothing about a preview either way — an assistant that accounts for what it had to do in order to obey is talking about itself.

cases.name: deploy with no section window open
cases.why: There is no button to press. This is the path Claude Code over MCP takes, and a deploy scheduled for half six in the morning. It must ask the same place for its launcher arguments as the button does, or a Cloudflare course goes to Netlify.

cases.name: deploy while that section is already busy
cases.why: A refusal in a whole sentence. The menu fragment that sits under a greyed-out menu item says nothing when read out in a conversation. Note the event: the assistant DOES press Deploy — the window is what declines, which is the real shape of it. This case was written expecting no event at all, and running it said otherwise.

cases.name: the deploy card is agreed to
cases.why: What the teacher chose is part of the history, in their own bubble. A conversation where the assistant asked, nothing answered, and something plainly happened is worse than one you cannot read back at all.

cases.name: the deploy card is cancelled
cases.why: The fact, and nothing else. Read which kind of card is pending BEFORE clearing it.

cases.name: a plan card is cancelled
cases.why: Here the reassurance IS the answer: the plan described changes to pages, so whether they happened is the part in doubt.

cases.name: a page edit, with a preview running
cases.why: The stop sits beside the WRITES, not beside the start: a preview left serving while the pages beneath it are rewritten serves a half-changed site, and the teacher's next refresh is a race they cannot see they are in. No expectReply on purpose — the reply is about the pages that changed, not about the preview; this case was written claiming the preview sentence, and running it said otherwise.

scenarios.note: What must happen, and in what ORDER. The order is the assertion: every wrong ordering still passes a test that only checks all three events occurred. Event names are this contract's own; map them to whatever your app calls them.

tools.note: Three lists, deliberately. `all` is what the runner can execute; `local` is what the small model is SHOWN (the plan twins and remember_timetable are taken off, because the model never has to name a plan and dates it supplies are dates it may have invented); `mcpOnly` is offered to Claude Code on top of everything, being the three that ask for judgement about meaning.
tools.planTwinsNote: A write with a twin is shown as a plan first. Four writes have none, deliberately: rebuild_preview changes no page, undo_last_change IS the remedy, deploy_section waits on its own button whatever plan mode says, and a cancelled scheduled deploy is remedied by scheduling it again.

function.description: TEACHERS SAY: "re-date my classes", "roll this section over to a new year", "put my classes on this year's dates". Re-date every class in a section onto the class dates on file, by POSITION — the first class takes the first date — and move the pages each class uses onto that class's day with it. Pages this section's Key Links points at move to the first day of class. Curriculum pages are left alone, because Plantoir dates those itself on every build. Set `website` when the teacher is rolling a section over to a NEW YEAR and has said which website they want: "new" starts a fresh one, so publishing no longer replaces last year's site, and "same" keeps last year's address. Ask them first — never choose for them, and leave it out for an ordinary re-dating.
function.name: re_date_classes
